articles.title: British author once faced a struggling 3,500-acre farm in Sussex before abandoning conventional farming; turned an estate into a wilding experiment
articles.summary: On a 3,500-acre estate in Sussex, the decision to stop farming conventionally did not mean simply leaving the land untouched.
articles.body: On a 3,500-acre estate in Sussex, the decision to stop farming conventionally did not mean simply leaving the land untouched. Isabella Tree and her husband, Charlie Burrell, began changing the way the Knepp Estate was managed, allowing large grazing animals to move across areas of the farm while reducing the interventions that had shaped the land for generations, as reported by Rewilding Institute. The change was partly driven by economics, but it also became an experiment in what might happen when natural processes were given more room. Over time, Tree describes soils recovering, earthworms returning and species that had become scarce appearing again. The estate became a working example of a different approach to land management.A 12th-century estate takes a new path under Isabella TreeKnepp had been part of the English countryside for centuries. Its history stretches back to the 12th century, while the Burrell family has been connected with the estate since the 18th century.By the late 20th century, however, farming the estate on its relatively small scale had become increasingly difficult to sustain. Tree and Burrell faced a choice between selling the land to larger farming operations or finding another way of making a living from it.They chose the second option. The decision was not presented as a plan to recreate some untouched version of the English countryside. Instead, the couple wanted to give natural processes more space while still managing the estate sufficiently to allow those processes to develop. Tree described the decision as a leap of faith.How grazing animals helped change the Knepp landscapeThe Knepp project used grazing animals to help reshape the landscape. Fallow deer, Old English Longhorn cattle, Exmoor ponies, Tamworth pigs and red deer were introduced to parts of the estate. Fences were removed in some places and added in others. A management plan was developed for the naturalistic grazing project, while Tree and Burrell sought advice from ecologists, ornithologists, foresters and other specialists.The animals were not being used merely as replacements for farm machinery. Their movement and grazing were intended to recreate some of the disturbances that would once have been produced by large herbivores moving through a landscape.Tree's account describes this as a way of restarting ecological processes rather than trying to dictate exactly which species should appear and where. That made the project different from a conventional conservation scheme with a fixed list of targets.When Knepp's weeds became part of the natural processThe shift required a different attitude towards what a farm should look like. Areas that might once have been kept tidy were allowed to become more untidy. Vegetation could spread. Some changes that appeared undesirable at first were left to develop rather than immediately being treated with chemicals or machinery.This approach was not always popular with neighbours. Tree recounts how the appearance of weeds, including a major spread of creeping thistle, prompted pressure to intervene. The concern was that the plants would spread beyond the estate and into neighbouring fields.Instead, the thistles eventually became part of another unexpected ecological sequence. Painted Lady butterfly larvae fed on them, helping to deal with the infestation without the herbicide treatment that had been considered.Earthworms return as Knepp's soil begins to regenerateSome of the most important changes were less visible than the returning birds and butterflies. The tree devotes particular attention to the soil. With fertilisers and pesticides no longer being routinely applied as they had been under conventional farming, earthworms returned and the soil began to regenerate.That shift mattered because the project was not simply about creating habitat on the surface. The condition of the soil was part of the wider ecological system being rebuilt. Instead of treating soil as a medium that could be maintained through continual inputs, the Knepp experiment allowed biological activity to become a larger part of the process.There was no single point at which the land suddenly became a functioning wild landscape. Tree describes a series of developments, some anticipated and many not.Wildlife began appearing in places where it had become scarceThe effects were visible across the estate. Tree describes increases in rare purple emperor butterflies and greater numbers of birds including nightingales and turtle doves. Species that had previously been absent or present only in small numbers began to return as the habitat became more varied. The grazing animals played a part in creating this complexity. Their movements helped produce a mixture of habitats rather than a uniform landscape, with different conditions developing alongside one another.That variety became one of the central features of the Knepp approach. Tree writes that introducing the right number and species of grazing animals could provide the initial push needed for natural processes to begin operating again. The idea was less about designing a finished landscape and more about setting conditions in which change could continue.A different relationship between farming and conservationTree's experience also challenges the idea that agricultural production and conservation necessarily have to occupy opposing sides of a land-use argument. Her account suggests that some land can be managed less intensively while still contributing to food production. Pasture-fed meat remained possible within the wider system, while areas less suited to intensive agriculture could be given greater freedom to develop ecological functions.That approach has also been presented as potentially useful to farming itself. Restored ecological processes can contribute to soil health, water resources and insect populations involved in pollination. For trees, conservation is therefore not only about protecting individual species. It is also about maintaining the systems on which landscapes and agriculture depend.Knepp became an experiment rather than a fixed blueprintThe estate's story between 2000 and 2018 forms much of Wilding, Tree's account of the transformation. What makes the experiment unusual is the extent to which its managers accepted uncertainty. They still monitored what was happening and worked with scientists and conservation specialists, but they did not attempt to control every outcome.A species might appear in unexpected numbers. A plant that looked like a problem could become food for an insect. Changes underground could precede more obvious changes above it. The result was a landscape shaped partly by intervention and partly by what happened after intervention was reduced.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Avanti West Coast services to be nationalised from March
articles.summary: The move is part of a plan to improve rail infrastructure, cut train delays and improve experiences for passengers.
articles.body:
Avanti West Coast train services will be nationalised from March next year, the government has announced.

"For years, we've heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price. Enough is enough," Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said.

The move is part of a government plan to improve rail infrastructure, cut train delays and improve experiences for passengers.

Avanti West Coast's managing director said he was "proud of what we've achieved over the last six years". The company's contract was due to come to an end on 7 March.

In a post on social media, Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed Alexander's comments.

"For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti's cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again," he said.

Andy Mellors, managing director at Avanti West Coast, said: "We're proud of what we've achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before."

He added: "Over the coming months, we'll work closely with the government to ensure a seamless transition into public ownership while remaining focused on delivering for our customers and communities."

In May, Avanti West Coast said one-in-seven rail services will be cut on its busiest routes following a government request to reduce spending.

The company - a joint venture between FirstGroup (70%) and Italian state operator Trenitalia (30%) - predicted the move would cause minimum disruption to passengers and not reduce revenues.

Companies such as Avanti West Coast have their finances heavily influenced by the Department for Transport (DfT) due to contracts introduced in March 2020 at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.

All train services operated under DfT contracts are being transferred to public ownership.

Great Western Railway - which is owned by FirstGroup - is to be brought under public ownership in December.

Several rail firms around the country are already publicly owned, including Great Anglia and South Western Railway. Welsh services were nationalised in 2021 and Scotland took trains into public ownership the following year.

articles.title: Jane Fonda conserved a New Mexico ranch before a 2018 easement protected 2,229 acres of habitat, farmland and nearly four miles of the Pecos River
articles.summary: Forked Lightning Ranch, in the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains near Pecos, New Mexico, has passed through notable hands over decades.
articles.body: Forked Lightning Ranch, in the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains near Pecos, New Mexico, has passed through notable hands over decades. Texas oilman Buddy Fogelson bought it in 1941; after marrying actress Greer Garson in 1949, the ranch became known for entertaining guests. Following Fogelson's 1987 death, Garson donated part of the property to the National Park Service, forming part of Pecos National Historical Park. Jane Fonda purchased what remained in 2000 and worked to conserve its natural communities until selling it in 2015. A conservation easement, completed by the New Mexico Land Conservancy in 2018, later protected 2,229 acres, including nearly four miles of the Pecos River.How has Forked Lightning Ranch protected wildlife habitat over timeAfter acquiring the remaining original ranch in 2000, Fonda worked to conserve and improve its natural communities. According to the New Mexico Land Conservancy, she continued this work until the property was sold to new owners in 2015.The Conservancy describes Forked Lightning Ranch as having important conservation values, including agriculture, scenic open space and wildlife habitat. The property also contains historic sites and includes nearly four miles of the Pecos River running through the ranch.How did conservation easements protect Forked Lightning RanchThe New Mexico Land Conservancy began protecting the ranch through conservation easements in three phases, starting in June 2010 and ending in October 2018. The Conservancy records the project as a donated conservation easement covering the ranch in San Miguel County.In October 2018, the Conservancy completed a new easement that added 403 acres to the existing protected area, bringing the total covered by the conservation easement to 2,229 acres. The new easement combined two previous easements with the additional acreage.What did the easement preserve at Forked Lightning RanchThe New Mexico Land Conservancy states that the easement protects the entire Forked Lightning Ranch and preserves the integrity of the property by removing the potential for selling off portions of the ranch in the future. The organisation identifies wildlife habitat, agricultural land and scenic open space among the property's conservation values.The Conservancy also notes that nearly four miles of the Pecos River run through the ranch and that several historic sites are located on the property. The completed 2018 easement therefore brought the previously protected areas and the additional 403 acres together under protection covering 2,229 acres of the ranch.You use AI every day. articles.body: CHANDIGARH: Several videos emerging from Lovely Professional University (LPU) in Punjab’s Phagwara appear to show students entering shops inside the university’s Uni Mall, picking up food, gadgets and other items amid the violent protests that rocked the campus on Sunday.In one video, a voice can be heard saying “free mein shopping, shopping done” as people move around inside a store.Another video shows a person pointing towards various items in the mall and saying, “What do you need? Order now, will get everything for you in free.”Also read: LPU Student Protest Live UpdatesOther visuals purportedly show students eating food items inside the mall, while another set of videos shows shops and other property damaged during the unrest.The videos could not be independently verified. It was also not immediately clear from the visuals whether all those seen taking items were students of LPU.The alleged looting came as protests at LPU over claims surrounding the alleged rape of a female student escalated into violence, with protesters vandalising property, attacking police vehicles and blocking NH-44.Police said protesters pelted stones at police personnel after they were asked to clear the highway blockade on Sunday evening. Two police vehicles were set on fire and several others were damaged, officials said. A number of policemen were injured in the clashes.Also read: Students atop MiG-23, military tankVideos circulating online also show damage to shops in the campus mall, an ATM kiosk and other university property. Some protesters were seen with their faces covered.According to police, messages about an alleged rape and the death by suicide of a female student had begun circulating on social media on Saturday night, following which students gathered outside a girls’ hostel. The protest later spread to the highway and other parts of the campus.Police said an FIR had been registered based on the complaint relating to the alleged rape and an SIT had been formed. Investigators said CCTV footage, forensic samples and call records would be examined as part of the probe.LPU, however, has denied the rape allegations being circulated on campus, describing them as “false, baseless and fabricated rumours”. The university said it would cooperate with the investigation.A student claimed that the situation had gone beyond the students’ protest and alleged that outsiders and “goons” had entered the university.“The university's stand is that the students should stay safe. Police eventually used a lathi charge to clear the blockade after negotiations failed, following which students allegedly retaliated with stone-pelting.Amid the violence, students were also seen climbing onto a decommissioned MiG-23 aircraft and a military tank displayed on the campus.LPU has suspended classes for 10 days from Monday and postponed midterm examinations until further notice.While some students alleged that outsiders were responsible for the looting, arson and vandalism, police said several people involved in the violence had their faces covered.The exact identities of those involved in the alleged looting and damage are expected to be established through CCTV footage and the police investigation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. articles.title: Anushka Sharma once took her ice-cream-loving daughter to an ice-cream museum and told her to eat as much as she wanted: Here’s what happened next and the takeaway for parents
articles.summary: For many parents, taking a child to an ice-cream museum and then saying, “Eat as much as you want,” may sound like the opposite of teaching healthy eating.
articles.body: For many parents, taking a child to an ice-cream museum and then saying, “Eat as much as you want,” may sound like the opposite of teaching healthy eating. But when Anushka Sharma tried it with her daughter Vamika, she noticed something that made her rethink the way children learn to regulate what they eat.Anushka, who has spoken openly about trying to build healthy food habits in her children from an early age, recalled the incident at an event in 2024. Her daughter, she said, loves ice cream and is “obsessed” with it. So when the opportunity came to indulge, Anushka decided not to impose a restriction.“I took her to an ice cream museum because she loves ice cream. She is obsessed. There, I told her, ‘Eat as much as you want.’ What happened next was what stayed with her.She didn’t eat that much,” Anushka said. “So, I think when you inculcate the right kind of habits in the beginning, they don’t stuff themselves with 10 ice creams. She must have had two, and then she was like, ‘I am done.’ So if you inculcate the right habits in the beginning, they’ll make the right choice,” she said.The incident offers an interesting window into a question many parents grapple with: Does constantly telling children that certain foods are “bad” or “not allowed” actually make those foods more tempting?Anushka’s approach: explain rather than simply restrictAnushka has described healthy eating as something she tries to teach through conversations rather than simply banning foods. She explained that she talks to Vamika about why different foods make the body feel different.“I think the only way I have managed to, and I am still trying, is that I do explain it to her. I tell her that there are some foods that give us energy so you can play and do different things. Some foods give that to us very quickly and then we have no energy left to do other things. Other foods give us energy in a way that we can keep playing,” she said.But she also admitted that a child does not necessarily accept every carefully prepared parental explanation.“I make it sound more interesting than I am making it to you guys right now. But I feel like she doesn’t buy most of the times, she is like, ‘Whatever, just give it!’” Anushka said.Her solution? Make the conversation playful.“I also pick days and give very lengthy explanations, which I try to make fun. I bring out the actress in me…” she added.That admission is perhaps one of the more relatable parts of her story. Teaching children about food is rarely a single conversation. Parents may explain, negotiate, repeat themselves and try different approaches- only to hear a child respond with an unimpressed “Whatever.”The ice-cream museum experience is particularly interesting because Anushka did not describe Vamika’s response as the result of a strict rule. Instead, the child was given an opportunity to have the food she loved without being told that she had to stop after a predetermined amount.Why calling food “bad” can complicate the conversationWhen parents repeatedly describe sweets, pizza, chips or ice cream as forbidden foods, children can begin to associate them with excitement precisely because they are restricted. On the other hand, presenting every food as equally nutritious would also be misleading.A more practical approach can be to help children understand that foods serve different purposes. Some foods provide nutrients needed for growth, while others are foods children can enjoy occasionally. The emphasis can remain on variety and balance rather than turning eating into a test of obedience.That is broadly consistent with what Anushka describes: she talks about energy, playing and how different foods affect the body, while also allowing her daughter to encounter foods she enjoys.Her earlier comments about family food routines also show that she places importance on consistency. In another September 2024 interaction, Anushka said she and Virat Kohli try to cook foods they grew up eating so that family recipes are passed on to their children. She also said she maintains fixed meal and sleep timings even while travelling, describing routine as a way of giving children “a sense of control.”The larger lesson for parentsThe ice-cream museum story is not really about whether a child should be allowed two ice creams, five ice creams or none. It is about what happens when parents move away from making food a battle.Anushka’s experience suggests that healthy eating habits may involve more than keeping junk food out of the house. Children also need opportunities to understand food, experience different tastes and gradually develop their own awareness of hunger and fullness.At the same time, every child is different. Appetite, age, sensory preferences, family routines and medical or nutritional needs can all affect eating behaviour. Parents should not interpret one celebrity parent’s experience as a universal formula.For Anushka, though, the surprise came in a simple moment: she gave her ice-cream-loving daughter permission to have as much as she wanted- and Vamika eventually decided she had had enough.Perhaps that is the part worth remembering. Sometimes the goal of teaching children healthy habits is not to make them afraid of the foods they love, but to help them understand their choices well enough that they do not need a parent standing beside them saying, “No more.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Wrestler Benjamin Satterley, known as 'Pac', dies aged 40
articles.summary: His death was confirmed just a day after he participated in an AEW match in Chicago.
articles.body:
British wrestler Benjamin Satterley, known as Pac, has died, his representatives have confirmed.

All Elite Wrestling (AEW) said it was "saddened to announce the passing" of Satterley, 40, who they said had signed with them in 2019.

The wrestler's death was confirmed just a day after he participated in AEW's "All Out" event at an arena in Chicago on Saturday evening.

"A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability," AEW said in a statement.

Satterley held multiple AEW Championships, and the organisation said he had competed in "some of the most memorable matches in AEW history".

Prior to his partnership with AEW, he also performed in World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), New Japan Pro-Wrestling and Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre in Mexico.

He had a number of different personas during his career including Pac, Adrian Neville and "The Man that Gravity Forgot". The latter was in reference to a signature finishing move which saw him spin 360 degrees from the top rope of the wrestling ring and land on his opponent.

Many of the tributes paid to Satterley have expressed shock at his death.

WWE Hall of Famer Paul Heyman described it as a "truly terrible loss" and said he was a "tremendous talent and even finer human being".

AEW President Tony Khan said he "defined excellence" as a husband, friend and in his wrestling knowledge, skill and "unprecedented athleticism".

"The greatest export from our country. Also the greatest human being," fellow British wrestler Will Ospreay wrote on X, sharing a photo of the pair in the ring together.

"I am in shock. This is heartbreaking," AEW wrestler Evil Uno said.

"We have lost another great person, a great soul, a true professional."

articles.title: Gareth Gates finds his Belle for Great Yarmouth pantomime
articles.summary: Rosanna Roscoe, whose family live in Norfolk, says the opportunity will be a "full circle moment".
articles.body:
A performer is ready to step into the shoes of a Disney princess after being selected from more than 200 hopefuls in a Norfolk theatre's first pantomime for 30 years.

More than 200 hopefuls auditioned in April for the opportunity to play the role of Belle in Beauty & The Beast at the Britannia Theatre in Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, over the festive season.

Rosanna Roscoe was announced for her first professional role opposite singing star Gareth Gates, who plays the cursed prince and is also co-producer.

She said: "The search for a local Belle was really important to the team... I have lots of family from Norfolk and my nan still lives there now."

Gates, who rose to fame on TV talent show Pop Idol in 2002 and has appeared in pantomimes for 15 years, has been working on the show for the past year with co-producer Brian Graves.

He said the team wanted to find a Belle locally to "transform someone's career from obscurity".

The audition panel received entries both in person and on film and whittled more than 200 auditionees down to five before Roscoe got the call.

Speaking to BBC Look East, she said: "My nan was probably one of the first people to witness any sort of performing ability.

"From the age of three I was dancing around the living room, running around the coffee table trying not to break all of her ornaments - it feels like a full circle moment to be back with my nan this Christmas and I'm living with her for the contract."

Gates said: "As soon as we saw Rosanna, we just knew and she has the most incredible voice and she is a great actress... we saw a lot of talent.

"A lot of our cast are homegrown, there's lots and lots of people from Norfolk.

"We are thrilled to have Rosanna and we can't wait to bring homegrown panto back to the Britannia Pier in Great Yarmouth."

The cast will have two weeks of rehearsals before the show opens on 8 December. It runs until 31 December.

articles.title: Banksy's flag statue's long-term future explored by council
articles.summary: Westminster City Council says it is the statue's custodian and is responsible for its safety.
articles.body:
Westminster City Council has said it is "exploring all options" for the future of Banksy's Blinded by the Flag statue in central London.

The street artist erected the statue of a man marching off a plinth with his face covered by a flag at Waterloo Place on 29 April.

Discussions about the artwork's future were held in the summer, but no decision was made. It will be discussed at an upcoming cabinet meeting, the Local Democracy Reporting Service understands.

The council has described itself as the statue's custodian and said it had been in contact with the street artist's team. Banksy owns the copyright but the council is responsible for the cost of keeping the statue safe.

A council spokesperson said: "Over the summer the council has been exploring all options for the Banksy Statue in Waterloo Place. No formal decision has been made about its long-term future."

The spokesperson did not state what options were being considered.

The statue is located just off the Mall and is near the statue of Florence Nightingale and Crimean War Memorial.

Critics interpreted the statue as a commentary on the consequences of blind allegiance to symbols.

In response to a Freedom of Information request from the BBC in August, the council said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and for a security guard to keep watch over it.

The artwork is largely undisturbed however its plinth has been defaced with a spray-painted tag.

articles.title: Pumpkin growers are feeling the impact of the summer heatwaves
articles.summary: What impact have the extreme heat and dry conditions over summer had on Halloween's pumpkin crops?
articles.body:
Pumpkins have become an essential part of Halloween, whether as haunting Jack-o'-lanterns or warming soups and pies, but has the extreme heat during the summer affected this year's harvest of the much-loved fruit?

Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record , with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F), beating the previous record of 34 days.

As a result of the drought conditions, growers have reported pumpkins, which need a plentiful water supply while growing, being smaller in size and ripening earlier than usual.

Eleanor Gilbert regularly shares her experiences of life on her family's Rookery Farm on the Hampshire-Berkshire border, on her Berkshire Farm Girl social media accounts.

The 24-year-old said her pumpkins were "50 or 60% down" on previous years.

She said: "I always overplant so I'll have enough but not the extra which I'd use for wholesale or for decorations.

"They're a lot smaller in size - pumpkins are 90% water and if they have had no water, they just haven't grown.

"As well as the drought, we're seeing potential issues with pollination - some of them have flowered again as they've tried to grow late. It could have been too hot for the bees during the summer.

"We've also seen a lot of weed issues. I've not seen this much weed before, normally the pumpkins can outgrow weeds."

As well as a tough summer for pumpkin growing, the family farm also suffered a dramatic field fire, which her stepfather tackled by using a combine harvester to create a fire break .

Rookery Farm is among many turning to staging pumpkin-picking events to generate extra income. Its Pumpkin Patch & Big Bale Play features pumpkin carving, a "magical golden pumpkin carriage" and other Halloween-themed attractions.

"Farmers have had such a tough time, three bad harvests in six years," she said. "With yields down, without the diversification, there wouldn't be an income.

"There's definitely going to be a different feel to the pumpkin patch this year - more bare patches and more weeds - but that's the authentic view of farm life, people will see the real impact of the drought."

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

Greg Klaes, a native of Detroit in the US, moved to a small holding near the Oxford Canal in the 1970s.

He specialises in growing Native American varieties of squash, sweetcorn and culinary pumpkins, selling to high-end and Michelin-starred restaurants in London.

He said he was "absolutely flabbergasted" that he managed to grow some 10 tonnes of pumpkins, given the weather conditions, which he put down to his organic farming practises and "regenerative methods".

"The crop came through, reduced by half on what I'd anticipated," he said. "I'm already planning irrigation for crops for next year."

His crop of multi-coloured Hopi sweetcorn was also down by a third on what was expected.

The National Farmers Union said it had been an "exceptionally challenging" season for pumpkin growers.

Horticulture and Potatoes Board chairman Martin Emmett said: "The prolonged hot and dry conditions created significant pressures, from establishing crops in the spring through to maintaining quality and yields as harvest approaches."

He said there would still be "plenty" of British pumpkins in the shops for carving but added that the heatwaves had been a "stark reminder" of the impact of the extreme heat.

"Ensuring growers have the confidence and support to invest in the future of a resilient and profitable British horticulture sector remains essential if we are to maintain domestic production and strengthen national food security," said Emmett.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said farmers had experienced a "difficult summer".

A spokesperson said: "Many have adapted innovatively by saving water for their crops but the drought brought huge challenges for the south of England.

"We are strengthening domestic food production and making it more resilient to future shocks."

Gardeners and domestic growers have also faced challenges trying to grow their own pumpkins this year.

The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) said the crop of pumpkins at RHS Wisley in Surrey appear to have "matured earlier than usual" after growing very quickly in the heat in August.

It said: "Fruits are on the small side but quality does not seem to have been affected and the fruits have coloured up well."

As pumpkins are native to the Americas, the society said they are well adapted to heatwaves, dry soils and future warmer, drier climates.

"They love heat and sunlight so the conditions were very good this summer," it added.

"They are not as thirsty as the closely-related cucumbers and courgettes, having surprisingly powerful roots.

"However, once the soil began to get dry in July, watering was very helpful although fair crops were possible without watering on good soils.

"Scientists are unravelling how these crops cope with drought and this will help breed more tolerant forms in time."

Add compost or rotted manure before planting, ideally as mulch 3-5cm (30-50mm) deep.

Sow or plant on level ground and make a pond for watering around the plants.

Mulch or manure should be enough feed but on poor soils, or if the plants are not growing well, add some seaweed fertiliser when watering.

To help with watering, grow in a shallow trench in sandy soils

Water at base of plants to discourage powdery mildew, a fungus disease encouraged by dry soil

Where space is very limited, consider the mini-pumpkins like Munchkin or Jill Be Little.

Let fruits ripen fully on the vine but once the neck is dry and cracking and fruits have a hard skin and ring hollow when tapped bring indoors into a cool but frost-free place.

Always harvest before frosts - they are ruined by even the slightest frosty nip.

Planting pumpkins on reasonably sunny compost heaps can give mighty crops as the pumpkin roots search the compost for water and nutrients.

With warmer early summer temperatures, consider sowing seeds direct in the soil instead of in pots, which should give better roots.

Nick Folkes, from Weston near Southampton, is one of the country's leading pumpkin carvers, each year creating designs for parties and corporate events.

Every autumn, he buys up to 20 pumpkins to carve, with many displayed outside his house on Halloween night.

"I like to push the boundaries, pushing it into more of an art form," he said.

He takes his inspiration from movie scenes, art works, celebrity faces or even places, but thinks this year could bring "challenges".

"In terms of size, looking at the fields, the pumpkins do seem smaller.

"There just hasn't been the rainfall. The ones in the supermarket will be smaller.

"You are constricted in the size of design and it tends to be more fiddly - the bigger the pumpkin, the more detail you get get on.

"For most people, doing eyes, nose and a mouth, you might need to find a smaller, sharper knife."

articles.title: Heat raises costs and cuts crop yields for Jersey farmers
articles.summary: Hot weather sees significantly smaller harvests and greater costs for farmers.
articles.body:
Farmers in Jersey say the hot weather has caused a number of problems this year, including significant reductions to their harvests and mounting watering costs.

At the beginning of September, Jersey Met Office confirmed this summer was the warmest since records began in 1894 .

Christine Hellio, from Manor Farm, said she had "never had to irrigate pumpkins to this extreme before". Meanwhile producers of apples and cereals said their harvests were down 90% and 50% respectively.

Assistant Environment Minister Kirsten Morel said the government was keen to speak to farmers and could look at reprioritising funds from its rural support scheme.

The Jersey Met Office said the average temperature for June, July and August was 20.5C (68.9F), compared to a 30-year average of 17.7C (63.9F) for these months.

It said the data was in line with evidence that climate change was driving hotter summers and increasing the likelihood of drier conditions.

Hellio, director of Manor Farms, said it was one of the businesses feeling the effect of the hot weather, which "had caused her a number of problems this year".

"I've never had to irrigate pumpkins to this extreme before... we'll still have pumpkins... but everything that we have grown this year has had to be irrigated a number of times over," she said.

Hellio said it meant an "added an extra expense on to every crop, as diesel has to be purchased to run the pumps".

"Nobody can control the weather but this year has been such an extreme. Where can we get some help to cover this expense for growing the crop," she said.

Kirsten Morel, Assistant Minister for Environment, Agriculture and Fisheries, said the government was keen to "sit down with the farming industry and understand what impacts the drought has had".

Morel said the money in the Rural Support Scheme was a fixed amount, but they could look to "prioritise things differently" in consultation with the industry.

Le Tâcheron Farm in Trinity grows cereals for things like baking and bread-making and farmer John Le Maistre said despite a wet start, the "very hot and very dry" summer had taken its toll.

It was "noticeable that the grain size was smaller than it would normally be" he said.

Le Maistre said this year's harvest produced half the amount of cereals compared to previous years.

In the UK, the harvest of things like cereal, oats and barley is said to be the worst since records began in 1984 .

Adrienne Le Maistre, senior meteorologist and forecasting manager at Jersey Met, said if the weather from recent years persists, it could challenge the notion that Jersey has a "northern temperate climate".

Le Maistre said it could "lead to a change in categorisation or how these categories are defined".

Regardless of the official designation, Le Maistre suggested that Jersey will continue to see "wetter, milder winters and hotter, drier summers".

Tim Crowley of La Mare Vineyard, in St Mary, described the summer weather as a "double-edged sword".

His apple orchards have seen the lowest crop for 50 years, producing "three or four tonnes of apples rather than the usual 60 or 70 tonnes".

Grapes have fared much better, but Crowley said "even for the vines, it's been too dry this year".

"We are seeing weather that's typical in Spain and the south of France, and we've never planted varieties for that climate... we base our planting on 30-year weather averages, but we're now looking at five-year averages because its changing that much and that quick," he said.

Cider producer, Paul Mellor says it's a similar story in Guernsey, where Rocquette Cider has faced an "appalling harvest...about 80% down".

Guernsey also saw its hottest summer on record in 2026.

Mellor said a bumper crop from the previous year had carried them through, but "two bad years would be devastating".

articles.title: University of Gloucestershire student living at home 'wasn't ready' to move away
articles.summary: A third of students starting courses are living at home, the University of Gloucestershire says.
articles.body:
A university says a third of students starting courses this year are living at home or commuting to lectures so they can be "financially better off".

The University of Gloucestershire said it had expanded support for students with flexible accommodation available for them to use, discounted travel and that it had created new facilities designed specifically for commuters.

Communications and media student Ofelia Bines grew up in Gloucester and, while she said she wanted to leave the city one day, she explained she "wasn't ready" yet.

"I know I'm better off financially compared to a lot of people living in halls," she said, adding "loads of people" were doing the same thing.

"Most people that I went to school with have stayed in the local area and gone to uni.

"For me, it just didn't make any sense to pay money for accommodation when I'm staying so close and still able to have friends and find that university experience is the best of both worlds," she added.

"I also couldn't leave my dog behind and being close to family is so important".

Taylor Barker, who has started her second year studying forensic psychology, makes a 40-minute commute to lectures at the university's City Campus in Gloucester.

She said studying from home was "a bonus" and financially it worked "out better to commute".

"My family are really important to me, I don't want to lose that connection from moving away," she said.

"It was quite scary, the thought of having to move."

She said she went to look at "a couple of universities a bit further away and I just didn't like it".

"It hasn't stopped me from being independent. You're meeting people in lectures, most of the time you'll find someone similar who commutes from either similar distances, or actually lives quite near you.

"It's just different ways of meeting people."

Stewart Dove, director of student experience at the university, said it was "sad" people were having to make decisions based around the cost of living, but commuting could help "manage the cost of university" and allow students to "continue with a part-time job or stay close to family and friends".

He added: "Our flexible accommodation at Pittville [campus] means students don't necessarily have to choose between moving away or commuting every day, they can live at home but have the option to stay close to campus for up to three nights a week.

"We hope that these options mean that commuter students are supported to easily access everything that the university can offer."

articles.title: Why your mind keeps you stuck
articles.summary: By Swami Sukhabodhananda One of life’s greatest prisons has no walls. It is the prison we createthrough our own way of thinking.
articles.body: By Swami SukhabodhanandaOne of life’s greatest prisons has no walls. It is the prison we createthrough our own way of thinking. The Upanishadic teaching says, “Atma va are mantavyah” – the Self has to be deeply reflected upon. Mantavyammeans to think, inquire, and contemplate.But all thinking is not of the same quality. Some thinking imprisons us; other thinking liberates us.We can understand this through three interesting words: tarka, kutarka and vitarka. Tarka is ordinary logic. It analyses, compares and reaches conclusions. Logic is useful, but on its own it can become dry. Life is much larger than what the logical mind can calculate. Kutarka is distorted or justifying logic. Here we do not use intelligence to discover truth; we use intelligence to defend what we have already decided to believe. The ego first reaches a conclusion and then employs the mind as its lawyer. “I became angry because he behaved badly.” “I cannot change because this is my nature.” “My unhappiness is because of my family.” “I failed because nobody supported me.”Notice the subtle mechanism. We are not investigating ourselves; we are defending ourselves. Watch many television debates. People often do not listen to learn. They listen to reply. Each side gathers arguments to strengthen an already existing position. That is kutarka.Unfortunately, we conduct similar debates inside ourselves. Then comes vitarka – breakthrough thinking. It asks, “What am i not seeing?”This is one of the great gifts Krishn gives Arjun in Gita. At the beginning of Gita, Arjun has arguments for withdrawing from battle. His arguments even sound noble and compassionate. Krishn does not merely give him another set of arguments. He changes the very dimension from which Arjun is looking at the situation. This is breakthrough thinking.Whenever you are disturbed, therefore, do not immediately believe the story your mind is telling you. Ask yourself three questions: What are the facts? What is my interpretation of those facts? Is there another way of seeing this situation?A fact is different from the story we build around it. Someone did not return your telephone call. That is a fact. “He does not respect me” is an interpretation. Once interpretation becomes reality, emotion follows. Anger appears, resentment grows, relationships suffer – and all because we confused our story with the fact.Spiritual intelligence begins when we create a little space between what happened and what the mind says happened. Krishn creates that space in Arjun.This is why, towards the end of Gita, Arjun declares, “Nasto mohah smrtir labdha” – my delusion has disappeared, and clarity has been regained.Notice Krishn has not changed the battlefield. He has changed consciousness of the person standing on the battlefield. That is the essence of transformation.We spend enormous energy trying to change people, circumstances and events. Certainly, external action is sometimes necessary. But before changing the world outside, ask: From what quality of mind am i looking at it? A conditioned mind can convert even an opportunity into a problem. An awakened mind can convert even a problem into a possibility.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Calls for Guernsey to make more of subsidised Paris air link
articles.summary: Hospitality boss says Aurignys Paris route is not being used to its full potential.
articles.body:
More could be done to attract visitors to Guernsey through its direct flight to Paris, according to the president of the island's hospitality association.

The route, operated by Aurigny under a States-backed agreement, has received its full subsidy in 2024 and 2025 after failing to meet revenue targets.

The Committee for Economic Development said the service had brought more than 2,000 visitors to the island and generated an estimated £1.4m in visitor spending.

Guernsey Hospitality Association president Alan Sillett said flights were at about 60% capacity, giving scope for significant growth.

Sillett said Paris was an important international hub and questioned whether Guernsey was making the most of the connection.

"Connectivity is massive for a small island and if we can pull the levers to get more major branded airlines in, let's do it," he said.

"The visitor economy can grow and one of the main levers is air connectivity."

The Paris route is being operated under a 36-month agreement designed to establish the service, with Aurigny receiving financial support if revenue falls below agreed targets.

Aurigny's chief commercial officer Philip Saunders said the airline was continuing to build a new market while facing higher operating costs, including fuel prices.

"We've been seeking to continue to give as good value as we can whilst at the same time building up a new market," he said.

Deputy Sasha Kazantseva-Miller, President of the Committee for Economic Development, said 2,021 visitors had travelled by air to Guernsey by the end of 2025 whose return journey originated in France.

Using the standard estimate of £693 spent per visitor arriving by air, she said the route had generated about £1.4m for the local economy.

"At the 21-month contract checkpoint, the Guernsey economic benefit from direct visitor spend was higher than the estimate on which the subsidy approval was based," she said.

The committee said higher operating costs and lower-than-expected ancillary revenue had affected the route's financial performance, but maintained its overall economic impact had been positive.

articles.title: Why are more towns and cities moving to 20mph?
articles.summary: Many councils are turning to 20mph limits, but questions remain over the benefits across the UK.
articles.body:
More councils across the UK are introducing 20mph speed limits on residential streets, arguing they save lives and make communities safer.

Critics say they increase journey times, add costs for businesses and can frustrate drivers.

As authorities consider wider rollouts, the debate over whether lower speed limits deliver enough benefits continues.

Wales introduced a default 20mph limit on most restricted roads in September 2023, while Edinburgh became Scotland's first city-wide 20mph network.

Across England, 20mph limits have become increasingly common and more than 30% of urban roads in Great Britain now have the restriction.

But the picture varies widely across the country, with London and parts of north-west England also embracing lower speeds.

Elsewhere, including parts of the West Midlands, East Midlands and South East, uptake has been far more limited.

Birmingham recently made headlines with plans to introduce 20mph limits on all non-A roads , although opponents have criticised the proposals as a "war on cars".

Coventry City Council is considering a broader approach to introducing lower speed limits, while Leicestershire County Council is consulting on similar plans, prompting debate among residents and councillors.

Supporters say the evidence increasingly points to safety benefits.

Research by the University of the West of England found average speeds fell by 2.7mph after 20mph limits were introduced in Bristol, while the Welsh government also reported reductions in vehicle speeds following its rollout.

Campaigners argue lower speeds not only reduce the likelihood of collisions but also make any crashes that do happen less severe.

Sue Nicholls, director of the charity 20's Plenty For Us, said lower speed limits could bring wider benefits, including reduced traffic noise, improved air quality and safer conditions for walking and cycling.

Prof Panos Georgakis, an expert in intelligent transport systems at the University of Wolverhampton, said the physics behind lower-speed collisions was clear.

"A vehicle travelling at 30mph has just over twice the amount of kinetic energy as one travelling at 20mph, so the force that will hit an individual is double," he said.

"If an accident takes place, the injuries will be much more serious, especially for vulnerable people such as the elderly or young children."

What do they mean for drivers and businesses?

Supporters argue lower speed limits can save motorists money.

The 20's Plenty For Us charity argues smoother driving at lower speeds can reduce fuel consumption in stop-start urban traffic, while fewer collisions could help lower insurance costs.

Critics, however, argue slower speed limits can lengthen journeys, particularly for delivery drivers and businesses that depend on road transport, while questioning whether they reduce congestion in practice.

Driving instructor Stuart Walker, from Wrexham, said some journeys now take significantly longer than before, reducing the number of lessons he can fit into a working day.

"Over five days, that's 200 pounds a week less. Every business is facing the same outcome," he said.

He believed wider 20mph rollouts could increase costs for businesses that rely on road transport and reduce productivity.

More than 6,500 people signed a petition calling for 20mph limits to be scrapped , arguing they slow traffic and increase congestion.

Department for Transport data published last year also suggested many motorists are struggling to adapt, with 76% of drivers exceeding the limit on monitored 20mph roads operating under free-flow conditions.

Opponents argue that lower limits should be targeted at roads with a clear safety risk, rather than introduced across large areas regardless of road layout.

Walker said he had noticed a rise in driver frustration since the Welsh changes were introduced.

However, he stressed that lower limits have a role in specific locations.

"It's a fantastic road safety tool outside schools, hospitals and housing estates," he said. "But to put it on roads where the speed reduction won't have any safety effect is wrong."

For some experts, the debate is no longer about whether 20mph speed limits are possible, but where they work best.

Georgakis said more evidence was needed to understand the long-term effects of widespread rollouts and whether blanket approaches are suitable everywhere.

As more councils consider lowering speed limits, policymakers face a balancing act between evidence suggesting safety benefits and concerns about costs, journey times and whether blanket 20mph limits are appropriate for every road.
